name: Joshua
v: When news of all this reached the kings west of the Jordan—those in the hill country, the lowlands, and along the entire Mediterranean coast as far north as Lebanon: the Hittites, Amorites, Canaanites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites—
they banded together to fight Joshua and Israel as one united front.
But the people of Gibeon heard what Joshua had done to Jericho and Ai,
and they decided to play it smart. They went out as a delegation in disguise—loaded their donkeys with worn-out sacks and cracked, patched-up wineskins,
wore beat-up sandals held together with stitching, threw on tattered clothes, and packed bread that had gone dry and crumbly.
In this state they showed up at Joshua's camp at Gilgal and said to him and the men of Israel, "We've come from a distant land. Cut a treaty with us."
The men of Israel eyed the Hivites and said, "How do we know you don't live right next door? If you do, we can't make any treaty with you."

They turned to Joshua: "We are your servants."

Joshua asked them, "Who are you? Where do you come from?"
They answered, "Your servants have traveled from a far-off country—because of the reputation of the LORD your God. We've heard the reports: everything he did in Egypt,
and what he did to the two Amorite kings east of the Jordan—Sihon of Heshbon and Og of Bashan in Ashtaroth.
So our elders and everyone back home told us, 'Pack supplies for the road and go meet them. Tell them: We are your servants. Make a treaty with us.'
Look at this bread. It was hot from the oven the day we packed it. Now it's dry and crumbling.
These wineskins were new when we filled them—now they're split. Our clothes and sandals are falling apart from the long journey."
The Israelites sampled the provisions—but did not consult the LORD.
Joshua made peace with them, cutting a treaty to let them live, and the leaders of the assembly swore the oath sealing it.
Three days after the treaty was signed, Israel learned the truth: these people were neighbors, living right in the area.
The Israelites marched out and on the third day reached their cities—Gibeon, Kephirah, Beeroth, and Kiriath-jearim.

But Israel didn't attack, because the leaders had sworn by the LORD, the God of Israel.

The whole community grumbled against the leaders,
but the leaders held the line: "We've sworn an oath by the LORD, the God of Israel. We cannot touch them.
Here's what we'll do: let them live, or wrath will fall on us for breaking the oath we swore."
The leaders added, "Let them live—but they'll cut wood and haul water for the whole community." So the leaders kept their word.
Joshua summoned the Gibeonites and confronted them: "Why did you lie to us? Why did you say, 'We live far away,' when you live right here among us?
Now you're under a curse. From this day on, you will always be slaves—woodcutters and water-haulers for the house of my God."

They answered Joshua, "Your servants were told plainly that the LORD your God had commanded his servant Moses to give you this entire land and wipe out everyone living in it. We were terrified for our lives because of you. That's why we did it.
Now we're in your hands. Do whatever seems right and fair to you."
So Joshua spared them. He kept Israel from killing them,
and that day he made them woodcutters and water-haulers for the community and for the altar of the LORD, at the place the LORD would choose—a role they hold to this day.

com.d:
# Joshua 9: The Cost of Hasty Decisions

Joshua 9 reveals a painful lesson about the dangers of making important decisions without seeking God's wisdom and counsel. The Gibeonites, facing certain destruction, devise an elaborate deception—donning worn clothes, carrying stale bread, and claiming to come from a distant land. Joshua and the elders examine their evidence and make a covenant with them, only later discovering they have been duped by neighbors who should have been destroyed according to God's command.

The tragedy here isn't merely that Israel was fooled, but that they neglected to consult the Lord. Verse 14 cuts to the heart of the matter: "The Israelites sampled their provisions but did not inquire of the Lord." This single sentence captures the spiritual carelessness that undermines countless decisions in our lives. Joshua had just witnessed miraculous victories at Jericho and Ai. The presence and power of God were undeniable. Yet in this moment, confronted with what seemed like straightforward evidence, he relied on human reasoning and failed to bring the matter to prayer.

We recognize ourselves in this mistake. How often do we examine the surface of situations—the credentials, the presentations, the apparent logic—and forge ahead without truly seeking God's guidance? We tell ourselves we don't have time to pray about every decision, yet the "small" choices often carry consequences as significant as Israel's treaty with the Gibeonites. The Gibeonites become servants in Israel's camp, a perpetual reminder of covenant made in haste.

Yet even here, God's sovereignty isn't thwarted. The covenant, made foolishly, becomes binding, and Israel honors it rather than breaking faith. There's a strange mercy in this account—God works within human failure rather than abandoning His people to their mistakes.

What decision are you facing today where you sense the pull to move quickly based on visible evidence alone? Before you proceed, would you pause to bring it genuinely before the Lord, trusting that His guidance is more reliable than your own assessment?
com.s:
Joshua 9 presents one of the most theologically complex narratives in the Deuteronomistic History, recounting how the Gibeonites successfully deceived Israel into making a covenant that contradicted the explicit divine mandate to destroy all Canaanite inhabitants. The chapter must be understood against the backdrop of Deuteronomy 7:1–2 and 20:10–18, which distinguished between distant cities (eligible for treaty) and local Canaanite populations (designated for complete destruction, *ḥērem*). The Gibeonites, a Hivite group inhabiting four cities northwest of Jerusalem, crafted their deception precisely around this distinction.

The narrative hinges on several key Hebrew terms that illuminate its theological concerns. The Gibeonites claim to come from a "very distant land" (*mēʾereṣ rəḥôqâ məʾōd*), directly invoking the Deuteronomic category that would permit covenant-making. Their elaborate ruse—moldy bread, worn sandals, cracked wineskins—serves as physical "evidence" of their purported long journey. The term *bərît* (covenant) appears prominently, and once ratified by oath (*šəbûʿâ*), this agreement becomes inviolable despite its fraudulent basis, demonstrating the ancient Near Eastern understanding of oath-sanctity that transcended circumstances of procurement.

The central failure identified by the narrator occurs in verse 14: the Israelites "did not ask direction from the LORD" (*wəʾet-pî YHWH lōʾ šāʾālû*). This phrase constitutes the theological crux of the chapter, indicating that proper discernment required divine consultation, likely through the Urim and Thummim or prophetic inquiry. The juxtaposition with the Ai narrative, where Joshua explicitly sought divine guidance, heightens the contrast.

Scholarly debate surrounds whether this narrative reflects historical memory of actual Gibeonite temple servitude or serves as an etiological explanation for the Gibeonites' later role as sanctuary servants (the *nətînîm* of later texts). The preservation of the Gibeonites creates ongoing tension within Israel's covenantal obligations—they must honor their oath while acknowledging its violation of divine command. This unresolved tension resurfaces in 2 Samuel 21, where Saul's violation of this covenant brings national consequences, confirming the narrative's enduring canonical significance regarding oath-keeping and its intersection with divine mandate.
com.p:
Joshua chapter nine unfolds approximately fourteen centuries before the coming of Christ, during the conquest of Canaan around 1400 BC. This event occurs shortly after Israel's stunning victories at Jericho and Ai, placing us squarely within the period of covenant fulfillment when God was giving Abraham's descendants the land He had promised six centuries earlier. On the grand arc of redemption, this moment stands between the Exodus deliverance and the establishment of the Kingdom, as Israel takes possession of her inheritance under divine warrior leadership.

The Gibeonites' deception presents a remarkable study in the interplay between divine sovereignty and human cunning. These Hivite inhabitants of Canaan, having heard of Israel's God-empowered conquests, resort to elaborate deception—moldy bread, worn wineskins, and tattered sandals—to secure a covenant of peace. The text delivers its verdict with devastating simplicity: the leaders of Israel sampled their provisions but did not inquire of the Lord. Here emerges a timeless pattern of spiritual failure—reliance upon human assessment rather than divine counsel, a sin that would plague Israel throughout her history and ultimately lead to exile.

Yet within this failure, sovereign grace weaves an extraordinary thread. The Gibeonites, though gaining their covenant through deception, genuinely believed that Israel's God was the true God of heaven and earth. Their confession in verse nine echoes throughout Scripture as pagan peoples recognize what Israel too often forgot. Typologically, the Gibeonites foreshadow the Gentile inclusion that would mark the new covenant age. Like Rahab before them, these Canaanites found refuge through faith—however imperfect—in Israel's God. They became woodcutters and water carriers for the tabernacle, perpetually serving at the place where heaven met earth, a role that prefigures the nations streaming to Zion in the latter days.

The binding nature of the oath Israel swore, even though obtained through deception, reveals something profound about covenant faithfulness. God held Israel to their word even when deceived, establishing that His people must be truth-keepers whose yes means yes. This anticipates the greater oath-keeper who would come—the faithful covenant Lord who keeps every promise despite humanity's unworthiness.

For the church dwelling between the advents, Joshua nine warns against practical atheism—making decisions without seeking the Lord's face. It simultaneously announces the glorious truth that God incorporates unlikely people into His covenant purposes, gathering worshippers from every nation to serve in His presence forever.
